pos: n. (Richard Vines, c. 1600–1656, Westminster divine, Master of Pembroke Hall, Cambridge)
etymology: Old German Ricohard, strong in rule; Vines, a dweller by the vineyards.
biblical_def: Richard Vines was a Leicestershire schoolmaster who became minister of Weddington, then of Watford and of St Lawrence Jewry in London, Master of Pembroke Hall at Cambridge, and one of the most respected members of the Westminster Assembly. His chief work there was on the Lord's supper and on church discipline; his Treatise of the Institution, Right Administration, and Receiving of the Sacrament of the Lord's Supper is the fullest Presbyterian statement of the subject from the Assembly years, and he defended the power of a church court to debar the scandalous from the table against the Erastian party, which held that the magistrate alone should decide. He was one of the ministers sent to attend Charles I at the Isle of Wight, opposed the regicide, and lost his mastership in 1650 for refusing the Engagement. He died in 1656 and so missed the Ejection. “But let a man examine himself, and so let him eat of that bread, and drink of that cup” (1Co 11:28) was the text he would not let go, for self-examination and church examination were in his view two sides of one duty.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a sacrament as an outward and visible sign of inward and spiritual grace, and to debar as to hinder or exclude from.
webster_full: SAC'RAMENT, n. An outward and visible sign of inward and spiritual grace.
DEBA'R, v.t. To cut off from entrance; to preclude; to hinder from approach.
EXAM'INE, v.t. To inspect carefully; to search or enquire into; to try by a rule.
scriptures: But let a man examine himself, and so let him eat of that bread, and drink of that cup.
For he that eateth and drinketh unworthily, eateth and drinketh damnation to himself, not discerning the Lord's body.
Ye cannot drink the cup of the Lord, and the cup of devils: ye cannot be partakers of the Lord's table, and of the table of devils.
And he saith unto him, Friend, how camest thou in hither not having a wedding garment? And he was speechless.
corruption_summary: Pembroke's master, the Assembly's fullest voice on the Lord's supper and discipline.
corruption_paragraphs: The Erastian position Vines fought is alive in a softened form wherever a church concludes that it has no business saying who may come to the table — that admission is a matter between the communicant and God, and any church judgment about it is an intrusion. Vines answered that Paul laid the duty on both: the man examines himself, and the church does not hand the elements to the openly scandalous.

The principle to recover is the seriousness of the ordinance itself: “he that eateth and drinketh unworthily, eateth and drinketh damnation to himself, not discerning the Lord's body” (1Co 11:29). A table from which nothing excludes is a table that proves nothing, and Paul will not let the Lord's table and the table of devils be held together (1Co 10:21).
roots_summary: Greek dokimazo (G1381), to prove, examine; diakrino (G1252), to discern; anaxios (G371), unworthily.
roots_lines: Greek dokimazo (G1381) — to test, prove, examine; 1 Corinthians 11:28.
Greek anaxios (G371) — unworthily, in an unworthy manner; 1 Corinthians 11:29.
usage: “But let a man examine himself” (1Co 11:28) — the communicant's duty.
“not discerning the Lord's body” (1Co 11:29) — against the Erastians.
“Friend, how camest thou in hither not having a wedding garment?” (Mat 22:12) — his argument for debarring.

pos: n. (Edmund Staunton, 1600–1671, Westminster divine, President of Corpus Christi College, Oxford)
etymology: Old English Eadmund, blessed protection; Staunton, from the place-name, the stone enclosure.
biblical_def: Edmund Staunton was vicar of Kingston upon Thames, a member of the Westminster Assembly, and from 1648 President of Corpus Christi College, Oxford, where he was put in by the parliamentary visitors and from which he was turned out at the Restoration in 1660. He was ejected again from his living in 1662 and ministered afterwards to a small Dissenting company at Bovingdon in Hertfordshire. He was a plain and fervent preacher, much given to visiting the sick and to catechising, and the funeral sermons he preached and that were preached for him describe a man whose chief characteristic was that he thought his office more honourable than his college. He had been well born and well provided and ended with little, and he reckoned the exchange profitable on the apostle's arithmetic: “Esteeming the reproach of Christ greater riches than the treasures in Egypt” (Heb 11:26). His own favourite word, often quoted by those who knew him, was the psalmist's: “I had rather be a doorkeeper in the house of my God” (Psa 84:10).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a doorkeeper as one who guards the entrance of a house, and reproach as censure mingled with contempt.
webster_full: DOORKEE'PER, n. One who keeps or guards a door; a porter.
REPROACH', n. Censure mingled with contempt or derision; abusive reflections.
PRES'IDENT, n. An officer appointed or elected to preside over a corporation or college.
scriptures: For a day in thy courts is better than a thousand. I had rather be a doorkeeper in the house of my God, than to dwell in the tents of wickedness.
Esteeming the reproach of Christ greater riches than the treasures in Egypt: for he had respect unto the recompence of the reward.

Yea doubtless, and I count all things but loss for the excellency of the knowledge of Christ Jesus my Lord: for whom I have suffered the loss of all things, and do count them but dung, that I may win Christ,
As sorrowful, yet alway rejoicing; as poor, yet making many rich; as having nothing, and yet possessing all things.
corruption_summary: Corpus Christi's president, twice turned out, who preferred a doorkeeper's place.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Staunton is a quiet rebuke to the way ministry is often measured, by the size and prestige of the post held. He presided over an Oxford college and ended in a village meeting with a handful of hearers, and the contemporaries who wrote about him thought the second half of that sentence the more honourable.

The principle to recover is the apostle's accounting, which is not resignation but calculation: “I count all things but loss for the excellency of the knowledge of Christ Jesus my Lord” (Php 3:8); “as having nothing, and yet possessing all things” (2Co 6:10). Moses made the same trade and had respect to the recompence of the reward (Heb 11:26).
roots_summary: Hebrew saphaph (H5605), to stand at the threshold; Greek oneidismos (G3680), reproach; zemia (G2209), loss.
roots_lines: Hebrew saphaph (H5605) — to stand at the threshold, be a doorkeeper; Psalm 84:10.
usage: “I had rather be a doorkeeper in the house of my God” (Psa 84:10) — his word, often quoted.
“Esteeming the reproach of Christ greater riches than the treasures in Egypt” (Heb 11:26) — 1660 and 1662.
“as having nothing, and yet possessing all things” (2Co 6:10) — Bovingdon.

pos: n. (Matthew Newcomen, c. 1610–1669, Westminster divine, one of the five authors of Smectymnuus)
etymology: Hebrew Mattithyahu, gift of the LORD; Newcomen, a newcomer, a stranger.
biblical_def: Matthew Newcomen was lecturer and then vicar of Dedham in Essex for nearly thirty years, a member of the Westminster Assembly, and one of the five Presbyterian ministers whose initials made up the pen-name Smectymnuus — Stephen Marshall, Edmund Calamy, Thomas Young, Matthew Newcomen and William Spurstowe — under which they answered Bishop Hall's defence of episcopacy in 1641. He was the youngest of the five and did much of the writing. He preached before Parliament, sat in the Assembly through its chief work, served on the committee for the Catechism, and was one of the Presbyterian commissioners at the Savoy Conference in 1661. Ejected in 1662, he accepted a call to the English congregation at Leiden and died there of the plague in 1669. His exposition of the Assembly's teaching on the ministry was that the office is Christ's gift to the church and not the crown's to define: “And he gave some, apostles; and some, prophets; and some, evangelists; and some, pastors and teachers” (Eph 4:11).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines episcopacy as government of the church by bishops, and a pastor as a minister who has the charge of a church.
webster_full: EPIS'COPACY, n. Government of the church by bishops; that form of ecclesiastical government.
PAS'TOR, n. A minister of the gospel who has the charge of a church and congregation.
PSEU'DONYM, n. A fictitious name assumed by an author.
scriptures: And he gave some, apostles; and some, prophets; and some, evangelists; and some, pastors and teachers;
And I will give you pastors according to mine heart, which shall feed you with knowledge and understanding.
For this cause left I thee in Crete, that thou shouldest set in order the things that are wanting, and ordain elders in every city, as I had appointed thee:
And when they had ordained them elders in every church, and had prayed with fasting, they commended them to the Lord, on whom they believed.
corruption_summary: Dedham's vicar, youngest of the Smectymnuus five, ejected and died at Leiden.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The Smectymnuus controversy is sometimes treated as a squabble over titles, bishop against presbyter, with Milton's pamphlets as the only part worth reading. The five were arguing something larger: whether the ministry is an order created by the church's head and described in Scripture, or an office whose shape the realm may settle for its own convenience.

The principle to recover is that the offices are given: “and some, pastors and teachers” (Eph 4:11), and God's promise is to “give you pastors according to mine heart, which shall feed you with knowledge and understanding” (Jer 3:15). What is given may be ordered (Tit 1:5) but not invented.
roots_summary: Greek didomi (G1325), to give; poimen (G4166), a shepherd, pastor; Hebrew ro'eh from ra'ah (H7462), to feed, shepherd.
roots_lines: Hebrew ra'ah (H7462) — to feed, tend, shepherd; Jeremiah 3:15.
usage: “some, pastors and teachers” (Eph 4:11) — the Smectymnuus case.
“I will give you pastors according to mine heart” (Jer 3:15) — Dedham for thirty years.
“ordain elders in every city” (Tit 1:5) — order, not invention.

pos: n. (Thomas Young, c. 1587–1655, Scottish minister, tutor to John Milton, one of the Smectymnuus five)
etymology: Aramaic Te'oma, a twin; Young, from Old English geong, young, a byname for the younger of two.
biblical_def: Thomas Young was a Scot of Luncarty, educated at St Andrews, who came south and in the 1610s was private tutor to the boy John Milton in London. Driven abroad by the hostility to Puritan ministers, he served the English merchants' congregation at Hamburg, and Milton's fourth Latin elegy is a letter to him there; the affection between them lasted, and Milton credited Young with his first serious learning. Returning in 1628, Young became vicar of Stowmarket in Suffolk, and in 1641 was one of the five ministers who signed the Answer to a Book entituled An Humble Remonstrance as Smectymnuus. He sat in the Westminster Assembly, was made Master of Jesus College, Cambridge, in 1644, and lost it in 1650 for refusing the Engagement; he returned to Stowmarket and died there in 1655. He also wrote a learned defence of the Christian Sabbath. His tutoring is his best monument. “Give instruction to a wise man, and he will be yet wiser: teach a just man, and he will increase in learning” (Pro 9:9).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a tutor as one who has the care of instructing another, and instruction as the act of teaching or information given.
webster_full: TU'TOR, n. One who has the care of instructing another in various branches of learning.
INSTRUC'TION, n. The act of teaching or informing the understanding; precept.
EL'EGY, n. A mournful or plaintive poem; a funeral song.
scriptures: Give instruction to a wise man, and he will be yet wiser: teach a just man, and he will increase in learning.
But continue thou in the things which thou hast learned and hast been assured of, knowing of whom thou hast learned them;
O God, thou hast taught me from my youth: and hitherto have I declared thy wondrous works.
Train up a child in the way he should go: and when he is old, he will not depart from it.
corruption_summary: Milton's tutor, Smectymnuus man, Master of Jesus College and vicar of Stowmarket.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Young is a reminder that the most consequential teaching is often the least recorded. He wrote a tract, sat in an assembly and held a mastership; but the lasting fruit of his life was the Latin and the piety he put into one boy in a London house, and no contemporary thought that worth describing.

The principle to recover is that instruction has a direction and a debt: “continue thou in the things which thou hast learned and hast been assured of, knowing of whom thou hast learned them” (2Ti 3:14). The teacher's own confession is the psalmist's — “O God, thou hast taught me from my youth” (Psa 71:17) — and the chain runs on from there.
roots_summary: Hebrew yasar (H3256), to instruct, discipline; lamad (H3925), to teach; Greek manthano (G3129), to learn.
roots_lines: Hebrew yasar (H3256) — to instruct, chasten, discipline; Proverbs 9:9.
Greek pistoo (G4104) — to be assured of; 2 Timothy 3:14.
usage: “teach a just man, and he will increase in learning” (Pro 9:9) — the boy Milton.
“knowing of whom thou hast learned them” (2Ti 3:14) — Milton's fourth elegy.
“O God, thou hast taught me from my youth” (Psa 71:17) — the tutor's own account.

pos: n. (jus divinum, the divine right; specifically the claim that presbyterian church government is of divine institution)
etymology: Latin jus, right, law, and divinum, divine — a right grounded in God's own appointment.
biblical_def: Jus divinum means a divine right, and in the seventeenth century it named the central question of the English church controversies: is the government of the church prescribed by Christ in Scripture, or left to the discretion of the magistrate and the wisdom of the age? The claim was made for episcopacy by Bancroft and Laud and for presbytery by the London ministers, whose Jus Divinum Regiminis Ecclesiastici of 1646 is the fullest statement — that the New Testament gives ruling elders, a plurality of elders in each congregation, and classes and synods of them for review, so that a church which adopts another form has not merely chosen differently but disobeyed. Against both stood the Erastians, who held that the magistrate governs the church, and the Independents, who granted a divine pattern but found it congregational. The Westminster Assembly took the presbyterian view and Parliament declined to enact it. The argument turns on whether texts like “the laying on of the hands of the presbytery” (1Ti 4:14) describe a binding institution or an apostolic custom.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines jus as law or right, and divine right as a right derived from God, not from human appointment.
webster_full: JUS, n. Law; right; a Latin word used in English law books.
DIVI'NE, a. Pertaining to the true God; proceeding from God.
REGIMEN, n. Orderly government; regulation; the government or management of a body.
scriptures: Neglect not the gift that is in thee, which was given thee by prophecy, with the laying on of the hands of the presbytery.
And when they had ordained them elders in every church, and had prayed with fasting, they commended them to the Lord, on whom they believed.
For this cause left I thee in Crete, that thou shouldest set in order the things that are wanting, and ordain elders in every city, as I had appointed thee:

Obey them that have the rule over you, and submit yourselves: for they watch for your souls, as they that must give account, that they may do it with joy, and not with grief: for that is unprofitable for you.
corruption_summary: The claim that church government is prescribed by Christ and not left to the state.
corruption_paragraphs: The modern instinct runs hard against jus divinum in any form. Polity is now widely treated as the adiaphora of the Christian life — a matter of taste, culture or efficiency, where the only sin is to insist. On that view a church may be led by a board, a bishop, a founder or a committee, and the New Testament offers no more than suggestions.

The principle to recover is that Scripture does in fact legislate here, whatever conclusion one reaches about the detail. Elders are ordained in every church (Act 14:23) and in every city (Tit 1:5); a presbytery lays on hands (1Ti 4:14); the flock is told to “Obey them that have the rule over you, and submit yourselves: for they watch for your souls” (Heb 13:17). A polity that cannot locate those men has a problem no appeal to liberty will answer.
roots_summary: Greek presbuterion (G4244), a body of elders; cheirotoneo (G5500), to appoint, ordain; hegeomai (G2233), to lead, rule.
roots_lines: Greek presbuterion (G4244) — the body of elders, presbytery; 1 Timothy 4:14.
Greek charisma (G5486) — a gift of grace; 1 Timothy 4:14.
Greek cheirotoneo (G5500) — to appoint by vote, ordain; Acts 14:23.
Greek kathistemi (G2525) — to appoint, set in order; Titus 1:5.
Greek hegeomai (G2233) — to lead, have the rule; Hebrews 13:17.
usage: “the laying on of the hands of the presbytery” (1Ti 4:14) — the text the argument turns on.
“when they had ordained them elders in every church” (Act 14:23) — the London ministers' case.
“Obey them that have the rule over you” (Heb 13:17) — a command that presupposes an order.

pos: n. (Philip Nye, c. 1595–1672, Independent divine, one of the Dissenting Brethren of the Westminster Assembly)
etymology: Greek Philippos, lover of horses; Nye, from Middle English atten ey, at the island.
biblical_def: Philip Nye was one of the five Dissenting Brethren — with Thomas Goodwin, Jeremiah Burroughs, Sidrach Simpson and William Bridge — who argued the Independent case in the Westminster Assembly against the Presbyterian majority, and whose Apologeticall Narration of 1643 put congregational principles before the English public. Having spent the 1630s in exile in Holland, he returned in 1640, helped frame the Solemn League and Covenant and administered it in London, and became one of Cromwell's most trusted ecclesiastical advisers, a Trier of ministers and a chief architect of the Protectorate's church settlement. He was excepted by name from the Act of Indemnity in 1660 and barred from public office, lived under threat, and ministered quietly in London until his death in 1672. His case against the Assembly was that the church to which Christ gives discipline is the gathered congregation: “And if he shall neglect to hear them, tell it unto the church” (Mat 18:17) means the local assembly, and no court above it.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines Independent as one who maintains that every congregation is a complete church, and a trier as one who tries or examines.
webster_full: INDEPEND'ENT, n. One who maintains that every congregation of Christians is a complete church, subject to no superior authority.
TRI'ER, n. One who tries or examines; one appointed to examine qualifications.
CONGREGA'TIONAL, a. Pertaining to a congregation; appropriated to the government of a single church.
scriptures: And if he shall neglect to hear them, tell it unto the church: but if he neglect to hear the church, let him be unto thee as an heathen man and a publican.
For where two or three are gathered together in my name, there am I in the midst of them.
Wherefore, brethren, look ye out among you seven men of honest report, full of the Holy Ghost and wisdom, whom we may appoint over this business.
In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, when ye are gathered together, and my spirit, with the power of our Lord Jesus Christ,
corruption_summary: The Independent leader of the Dissenting Brethren and Cromwell's church adviser.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Nye's dispute with the Presbyterians is often flattened into a modern preference for local autonomy, as though the Dissenting Brethren were arguing that each church should be left alone. They were arguing from texts, and conceding a great deal: that there is a divine pattern, that discipline is real and binding, and that a congregation which will not exercise it has failed.

The principle both sides held, and which the modern version of congregationalism often loses, is that the local church has authority and must use it: “tell it unto the church” (Mat 18:17); and “where two or three are gathered together in my name, there am I in the midst of them” (Mat 18:20) is said in the context of that discipline, not of a prayer meeting's attendance.
roots_summary: Greek ekklesia (G1577), an assembly called out; episkeptomai (G1980), to look out, select; sunago (G4863), to gather together.
roots_lines: Greek parakouo (G3878) — to neglect to hear, disobey; Matthew 18:17.
Greek episkeptomai (G1980) — to look out, select; Acts 6:3.
usage: “tell it unto the church” (Mat 18:17) — the Dissenting Brethren's text.
“there am I in the midst of them” (Mat 18:20) — the Apologeticall Narration, 1643.
“look ye out among you seven men of honest report” (Act 6:3) — a congregation choosing its officers.

pos: n. (Sidrach Simpson, c. 1600–1655, Independent divine, Master of Pembroke Hall, one of the Dissenting Brethren)
etymology: Hebrew Shadrach, the Babylonian name given to Hananiah; Simpson, son of Simon.
biblical_def: Sidrach Simpson was a Cambridge man who served a London lectureship, was silenced for nonconformity under Laud, and went into exile in Holland, where he ministered first with Thomas Goodwin at Arnhem and then separately. He returned in 1641 and became one of the five Dissenting Brethren in the Westminster Assembly, a signatory of the Apologeticall Narration, and pastor of a gathered church at St Mary Abchurch in London. Cromwell appointed him Master of Pembroke Hall, Cambridge, in 1650 and he was one of the Triers. He was the most rigorous separatist of the five: he had broken with Goodwin in Holland over the strictness of admission to the church, holding that a congregation is composed only of visible saints who can give an account of a work of grace, and in England he applied the same standard. He died in 1655 while attending a sick parishioner. His governing text was Paul's to the Corinthians: “Wherefore come out from among them, and be ye separate, saith the Lord” (2Co 6:17).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines separation as the act of parting or disuniting, and a saint as a person sanctified, a holy or godly person.
webster_full: SEPARA'TION, n. The act of separating; disjunction; the state of being separate.
SAINT, n. A person sanctified; a holy or godly person; one eminent for piety and virtue.
ADMIS'SION, n. The act or practice of admitting; access; entrance.
scriptures: Wherefore come out from among them, and be ye separate, saith the Lord, and touch not the unclean thing; and I will receive you,
And if he shall neglect to hear them, tell it unto the church: but if he neglect to hear the church, let him be unto thee as an heathen man and a publican.
As they ministered to the Lord, and fasted, the Holy Ghost said, Separate me Barnabas and Saul for the work whereunto I have called them.
For where two or three are gathered together in my name, there am I in the midst of them.
corruption_summary: The strictest of the Dissenting Brethren, Master of Pembroke Hall and a Trier.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Simpson's rigour is the point at which congregational principle becomes a pastoral problem, and he saw it clearly. If the church is the company of visible saints, somebody must judge the visibility, and that judgment will sometimes shut out the timid believer while admitting the articulate hypocrite. He broke with his closest colleague over it.

The principle to recover is that both halves of the tension are scriptural. The call to separation is real and is addressed to a church, not only to an individual (2Co 6:17); and the discipline that follows presupposes a body able to receive a report and act on it (Mat 18:17). A church that admits everyone has no discipline; a church that admits almost no one has no mercy.
roots_summary: Greek aphorizo (G873), to separate, set apart; hagios (G40), holy, a saint; leitourgeo (G3008), to minister.
roots_lines: Greek aphorizo (G873) — to separate, mark off, set apart; 2 Corinthians 6:17.
Greek leitourgeo (G3008) — to minister, serve publicly; Acts 13:2.
usage: “come out from among them, and be ye separate” (2Co 6:17) — his governing text.
“As they ministered to the Lord, and fasted” (Act 13:2) — a gathered church's calling of officers.
“tell it unto the church” (Mat 18:17) — discipline in a company of visible saints.

pos: n. (Edmund Grindal, c. 1519–1583, Archbishop of Canterbury, sequestered for refusing to suppress the prophesyings)
etymology: Old English Eadmund, blessed protection; Grindal, from the Cumberland place-name, the green valley.
biblical_def: Edmund Grindal was a Cumberland man, a Marian exile at Strasbourg and Frankfurt, then successively Bishop of London, Archbishop of York and, from 1575, Archbishop of Canterbury. He was the most Reformed of the Elizabethan primates and the only one who tried to govern the English church as a preaching church. His ruin came over the prophesyings — local conferences at which clergy expounded Scripture in turn before their brethren and often before the people, for mutual instruction in a church where most parish ministers could barely preach at all. Elizabeth, suspecting them as seedbeds of faction, ordered Grindal to suppress them and to reduce the number of preachers. He refused, and wrote her a long letter of December 1576 in which he declined to execute the order, reminded her that she was mortal and would answer to God, and asked her to refer such matters to the bishops. She sequestered him from his jurisdiction for the rest of his life. “We ought to obey God rather than men” (Act 5:29) was never more deliberately said by an English archbishop.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines to prophesy as to preach or instruct in religious doctrine, and to sequester as to separate from the owner for a time.
webster_full: PROPH'ESY, v.i. To utter predictions; to preach; to instruct in religious doctrines.
SEQUES'TER, v.t. To separate from the owner for a time; to seize or take possession of.
PRI'MATE, n. The chief ecclesiastic in a national church; an archbishop.
scriptures: Then Peter and the other apostles answered and said, We ought to obey God rather than men.
For ye may all prophesy one by one, that all may learn, and all may be comforted.
Behold, the days come, saith the Lord GOD, that I will send a famine in the land, not a famine of bread, nor a thirst for water, but of hearing the words of the LORD:
corruption_summary: The archbishop who refused Elizabeth's order to suppress the prophesyings.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Grindal's letter deserves to be better known because of who wrote it: not a Puritan pamphleteer with nothing to lose, but the Queen's own primate, at the height of his office, telling his sovereign that he could not obey her in this and that she would die and be judged. He kept the see and lost the use of it, which is the price such letters usually cost.

The principle to recover is that preaching is not a quantity a state may regulate downward: “For ye may all prophesy one by one, that all may learn, and all may be comforted” (1Co 14:31). Amos names the judgment Grindal feared — “a famine in the land, not a famine of bread, nor a thirst for water, but of hearing the words of the LORD” (Amo 8:11) — and the apostle's rule is short: “Quench not the Spirit” (1Th 5:19).
roots_summary: Greek propheteuo (G4395), to prophesy, preach; sbennumi (G4570), to quench; Hebrew ra'ab (H7458), famine.
roots_lines: Greek propheteuo (G4395) — to prophesy, speak forth; 1 Corinthians 14:31.
usage: “We ought to obey God rather than men” (Act 5:29) — the letter of December 1576.
“ye may all prophesy one by one, that all may learn” (1Co 14:31) — the prophesyings defended.
“not a famine of bread, nor a thirst for water, but of hearing the words of the LORD” (Amo 8:11) — what he feared from fewer preachers.

pos: n. (Richard Hooker, 1554–1600, author of the Laws of Ecclesiastical Polity, the classic defence of the Elizabethan settlement)
etymology: Old German Ricohard, strong in rule; Hooker, a maker or user of hooks.
biblical_def: Richard Hooker was Master of the Temple and afterwards rector of Bishopsbourne, and the author of Of the Laws of Ecclesiastical Polity, published from 1593, the most considerable work of theology written in English in the sixteenth century and the foundation of a distinctively Anglican method. Against Thomas Cartwright and the presbyterians, who held that Scripture prescribes a form of church government and that whatever is not commanded is forbidden, Hooker argued that Scripture is sufficient for salvation but does not legislate on every matter; that in things indifferent the church may order its own affairs by reason, law and custom; and that the long consent of the church carries real weight. From that follow the characteristic Anglican appeals to reason and tradition alongside Scripture. Reformed readers owe Hooker the respect due to a great and honest mind, and must still answer him: his argument gives the church a liberty in worship and order that Scripture does not plainly grant. “To the law and to the testimony: if they speak not according to this word, it is because there is no light in them” (Isa 8:20).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines polity as the form of civil or ecclesiastical government, and indifferent as neither right nor wrong, of no moral consequence.
webster_full: POL'ITY, n. The form or constitution of civil government; also, the constitution of a church.
INDIF'FERENT, a. Neither good nor bad; of no moral consequence; neutral.
TRADI'TION, n. The delivery of opinions, doctrines or customs from father to son, by oral communication.
scriptures: To the law and to the testimony: if they speak not according to this word, it is because there is no light in them.
All scripture is given by inspiration of God, and is profitable for doctrine, for reproof, for correction, for instruction in righteousness:
But in vain they do worship me, teaching for doctrines the commandments of men.
Beware lest any man spoil you through philosophy and vain deceit, after the tradition of men, after the rudiments of the world, and not after Christ.
corruption_summary: The great defender of the Elizabethan settlement, and the argument Reformed churches must answer.
corruption_paragraphs: Hooker is the ancestor of the three-legged stool — Scripture, tradition and reason — and his modern admirers often use it in a way he would not have: to make Scripture one voice among three, so that reason or the settled practice of the age may overrule a plain text. Hooker held Scripture to be supreme and infallible; he denied that it was exhaustive about order. The slide from the second claim to the first is not his, but it is made in his name.

The principle to recover is the test Isaiah lays down for any appeal: “To the law and to the testimony: if they speak not according to this word, it is because there is no light in them” (Isa 8:20). Where Scripture does speak, custom yields; and Paul's warning about “the tradition of men, after the rudiments of the world” (Col 2:8) is a warning to churches with long memories.
roots_summary: Hebrew torah (H8451), law, instruction; teudah (H8584), testimony; Greek theopneustos (G2315), God-breathed.
roots_lines: Greek paradosis (G3862) — tradition, what is handed down; Colossians 2:8.
usage: “To the law and to the testimony” (Isa 8:20) — the Reformed answer to the Laws.
“All scripture is given by inspiration of God” (2Ti 3:16) — which Hooker granted in full.
“teaching for doctrines the commandments of men” (Mat 15:9) — the risk in things indifferent.

pos: n. (John Field, c. 1545–1588, London preacher, co-author of the Admonition to the Parliament and organiser of the presbyterian movement)
etymology: Hebrew Yochanan, the LORD is gracious; Field, from Old English feld, open land.
biblical_def: John Field was the organiser of the Elizabethan presbyterian movement and, with Thomas Wilcox, the author of An Admonition to the Parliament of 1572, the manifesto that first demanded of an English parliament the abolition of episcopacy and the establishment of presbyteries. Both men went to Newgate for it. Field was a London preacher, lecturer at Holy Trinity Minories, and above all a man of business: he kept the correspondence of the movement, collected the Register of its documents and of the sufferings of its ministers, organised the classes that met in secret through the 1580s, and coordinated the parliamentary campaigns. Whitgift's subscription drive silenced him repeatedly and he died in 1588, before the movement was broken. Hooker and his party dated the whole controversy from the Admonition, and they were right to. Field wanted a church ordered by the New Testament pattern and nothing else: “that thou shouldest set in order the things that are wanting, and ordain elders in every city” (Tit 1:5).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines an admonition as gentle reproof or counselling against a fault, and a classis as an assembly or convention of pastors.
webster_full: ADMONI'TION, n. Gentle reproof; counselling against a fault; instruction in duties.
CLAS'SIS, n. In ecclesiastical affairs, an assembly or convention of pastors; a presbytery.
REG'ISTER, n. A written account or entry; a book of records.
scriptures: For this cause left I thee in Crete, that thou shouldest set in order the things that are wanting, and ordain elders in every city, as I had appointed thee:
And when they had ordained them elders in every church, and had prayed with fasting, they commended them to the Lord, on whom they believed.
Thus saith the LORD, Stand ye in the ways, and see, and ask for the old paths, where is the good way, and walk therein, and ye shall find rest for your souls. But they said, We will not walk therein.
But in vain they do worship me, teaching for doctrines the commandments of men.
corruption_summary: The organiser of Elizabethan presbyterianism and co-author of the 1572 Admonition.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Field is a useful corrective to the way reform movements are remembered. The names that survive are the writers and the martyrs; the man who kept the letters, built the register, arranged the meetings and timed the parliamentary bills is forgotten, and without him there would have been nothing for the writers to defend.

The principle to recover is that a church's order is something to be set right deliberately: “set in order the things that are wanting, and ordain elders in every city” (Tit 1:5). The old paths are to be asked for and then walked in (Jer 6:16), which takes organisation as well as conviction; and against the alternative stands the Lord's own verdict on worship built from men's commandments (Mat 15:9).
roots_summary: Greek epidiorthoo (G1930), to set further in order; leipo (G3007), to be wanting; Hebrew nathib (H5410), a path.
roots_lines: Greek epidiorthoo (G1930) — to set further in order, correct; Titus 1:5.
Greek leipo (G3007) — to lack, be wanting; Titus 1:5.
Hebrew nathib (H5410) — a path, trodden way; Jeremiah 6:16.
Greek entalma (G1778) — a commandment of men; Matthew 15:9.
usage: “set in order the things that are wanting” (Tit 1:5) — the Admonition of 1572.
“when they had ordained them elders in every church” (Act 14:23) — the secret classes.
“ask for the old paths, where is the good way” (Jer 6:16) — and then organise.
